idiom_name: std::variant<...> with std::visit over an overloaded visitor
implementation_notes: The closed set becomes std::variant<A, B, C> and dispatch becomes std::visit, whose requirements make coverage a compile-time obligation: the standard mandates that the visitor be callable for every alternative, so an overload set that misses one fails to compile. Prefer the overloaded/heritage helper with one lambda per variant over a single generic lambda with an if constexpr chain, because the explicit overload set gives the coverage error and blocks silent implicit conversions. Keep the classic visitor when the set must stay open to third-party subtypes, and use std::get_if or holds_alternative only for single-alternative queries.
pitfalls: std::visit accepts any callable valid for all alternatives, so a generic [](auto&&) lambda or a catch-all base-class overload silently removes the coverage check.
A variant that threw during a type-changing assignment becomes valueless_by_exception, and visiting it throws std::bad_variant_access; handle that as a boundary failure.
Overload resolution binds by best match: an int alternative can bind to a double overload, so take the exact alternative type (const Circle&) rather than a value parameter.

variants.name: Boost.Variant + apply_visitor (pre-C++17)
variants.idiom_name: boost::variant with boost::apply_visitor and a static_visitor subclass
variants.implementation_notes: Before std::variant, Boost.Variant provided the bounded discriminated union and apply_visitor provided compile-time checked visitation: the documentation states that visitation requires the programmer to handle (or ignore) each bounded type and that failing to do so is a compile-time error. That makes it the portable variant/visit realization for toolchains stuck before C++17, at the cost of a heavier header dependency and notoriously long template diagnostics. Use it only where std::variant is unavailable: the standard library version has the same semantics with better errors and no third-party dependency.
pitfalls: The coverage check depends on the StaticVisitor concept, so a template operator()(T&) overload accepts every bounded type and quietly erases the guarantee.
boost::variant is a legacy dependency once std::variant exists; keep it only for pre-C++17 toolchains, and expect very long compiler diagnostics when a visit is incomplete.

variants.name: Classic double dispatch: abstract accept + visitor overloads
variants.idiom_name: abstract Shape::accept(Visitor&) with a pure-virtual overload per variant
variants.implementation_notes: The object-oriented realization of exhaustive case analysis: each variant is a class deriving from an abstract base whose accept(Visitor&) calls the matching visit overload, and each operation is a visitor subclass with one override per variant. Coverage is enforced by the compiler in the other direction - a missing override leaves the visitor abstract, so the translation unit does not compile, which is exactly the guarantee std::visit gives over a variant. Choose this when the hierarchy must stay extensible by other translation units or when operations need privileged access to variant internals; it costs one class per operation and a virtual call per dispatch.
pitfalls: Coverage holds only while the visitor declares the overload set as pure virtual; a default empty visit() overload hides every missing variant.
Ownership and slicing: store variants behind smart pointers and give the base a virtual destructor, or derived payloads are sliced on copy or leaked on delete.
Every new operation means a new visitor class plus accept plumbing on all variants, the cost that variant visitation reverses.
